steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on boundary-aware uncertainty for feature attribution explainers. Motivate why explanation uncertainty matters, explain why decision boundary complexity is a missing source of uncertainty, introduce our kernel and GP-based framework, and list the contributions.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Post-hoc explainability methods have become an important tool for understanding and diagnosing the predictions of black-box models. Recently many of these explainers have been introduced in the category of local feature attribution methods, which are methods that return a real-valued score for each feature that represents its relative importance for the model prediction. These explainers are local because they are not limited to using the same decision rules over the whole data distribution, so they can better represent nonlinear and complex black-box models.

But recent works have shown that local explainers can be inconsistent or unstable. For example, explainers can give very dissimilar explanations for similar samples, be sensitive to imperceptible perturbations, or not be stable when applied repeatedly. In high-stakes applications it is necessary to give the user an understanding of whether an explanation is reliable, potentially problematic, or even misleading. One way to guide users about how reliable an explainer is, is to provide corresponding uncertainty quantification estimates.

Explainers can be considered as function approximators, so the standard techniques for quantifying the uncertainty of estimators can be used to quantify the uncertainty of explainers. This is the strategy used by existing methods that estimate explainer uncertainty. However, we observe that for explainers this is not enough. Besides the uncertainty coming from the function approximation of explainers, explainers also have to deal with uncertainty that comes from the complexity of the decision boundary (DB) of the black-box model in the local region that is being explained.

- DB geometry and motivating example
  - higher DB complexity related to increased generalization error and adversarial vulnerability
  - smoother DBs: better feature attributions, more consistent counterfactual explanations
  - ReLU networks: similar predictions can give widely disparate explanations; regulated through model smoothing
  - Fig. 1: medical diagnosis model, two features: cholesterol level, sodium intake
  - gradient per feature as importance estimate
  - patients A and B: similar levels, same prediction; complex DB (left) -> different top feature; smoothed DB (right) -> more consistent

- WEG kernel and GPEC
  - similarity perspective: given two samples and explanations, how closely related should explanations be?
  - similarity defined geometrically from DB complexity between the two points
  - Weighted Exponential Geodesic (WEG) kernel: samples close in Euclidean space may not be similar if local DB highly complex
  - Gaussian Process Explanation UnCertainty (GPEC) framework (Fig. 2): instance-wise, model-agnostic, explainer-agnostic
  - complementary to existing methods, which capture function approximation uncertainty (model parameters, explainer fitting) but not DB complexity
  - GPEC combines DB-based uncertainty with function approximation uncertainty from any local feature attribution method

- Contributions
  - geometric perspective on explanation uncertainty; geodesic-based similarity between explanations; proof it captures DB complexity of a black-box classifier
  - Gaussian Process-based framework combining 1) DB complexity uncertainty and 2) explainer-specific function approximation uncertainty, for any feature attribution method and black box model
  - empirical results: GPEC uncertainty improves understanding of feature attribution methods

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Post-hoc explainability methods have become an important tool for understanding and diagnosing the predictions of black-box models. Recently many of these explainers have been introduced in the category of local feature attribution methods, which are methods that return a real-valued score for each feature that represents its relative importance for the model prediction. These explainers are local because they are not limited to using the same decision rules over the whole data distribution, so they can better represent nonlinear and complex black-box models.

But recent works have shown that local explainers can be inconsistent or unstable. For example, explainers can give very dissimilar explanations for similar samples, be sensitive to imperceptible perturbations, or not be stable when applied repeatedly. In high-stakes applications it is necessary to give the user an understanding of whether an explanation is reliable, potentially problematic, or even misleading. One way to guide users about how reliable an explainer is, is to provide corresponding uncertainty quantification estimates.

Explainers can be considered as function approximators, so the standard techniques for quantifying the uncertainty of estimators can be used to quantify the uncertainty of explainers. This is the strategy used by existing methods that estimate explainer uncertainty. However, we observe that for explainers this is not enough. Besides the uncertainty coming from the function approximation of explainers, explainers also have to deal with uncertainty that comes from the complexity of the decision boundary (DB) of the black-box model in the local region that is being explained.

Previous works that look at DB geometry have related higher DB complexity to increased model generalization error and increased adversarial vulnerability. It has been shown that smoother DBs improve feature attributions and give more consistent counterfactual explanations. Another work shows that in ReLU networks, samples with similar predictions can have widely disparate explanations, and that this can be regulated through model smoothing. As an example (Fig. 1), consider a prediction model that is used for a medical diagnosis with two features: cholesterol level and sodium intake. We use the gradient with respect to each feature as an estimate of the feature importance. Patients A and B have similar cholesterol and sodium levels and they get the same prediction, but because of the complex decision boundary (left) each patient gets a different top feature. On the other hand, the smoothed decision boundary (right) gives more consistent explanations.

We look at this problem from the perspective of similarity: if we have two samples and their explanations, how closely related should the explanations be? Based on the intuition above, we define this similarity from a geometric perspective of the DB complexity between the two points. Specifically, we propose the new Weighted Exponential Geodesic (WEG) kernel, which encodes our expectation that two samples that are close in Euclidean space may not actually be similar if the DB in a local neighborhood of the samples is highly complex.

Using this similarity formulation, we propose the G aussian P rocess E xplanation Un C ertainty (GPEC) framework (Fig. 2), which is an instance-wise, model-agnostic, and explainer-agnostic method for quantifying explanation uncertainty. This notion of uncertainty is complementary to the existing quantification methods. The existing methods mostly estimate the uncertainty related to the choice of model parameters and fitting the explainer, which we call function approximation uncertainty, and they do not capture the uncertainty related to DB complexity. GPEC can combine the DB-based uncertainty with function approximation uncertainty from any local feature attribution method.

To summarize, our contributions are the following:

- • We introduce a new geometric perspective on capturing explanation uncertainty and we define a geodesic-based similarity between explanations. We prove theoretically that this similarity captures the complexity of the decision boundary of a given black-box classifier.

- • We propose a new Gaussian Process-based framework that combines 1) uncertainty from decision boundary complexity and 2) explainer-specific function approximation uncertainty, to generate uncertainty estimates for any given feature attribution method and black box model.

- • Our empirical results show that GPEC uncertainty improves the understanding of feature attribution methods.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Post-hoc explainability methods have become a crucial tool for understanding and diagnosing black-box model predictions. Recently, many such explainers have been introduced in the category of local feature attribution methods, that is, methods that return a real-valued score representing each feature’s relative importance for the model prediction. These explainers are local in that they are not limited to using the same decision rules throughout the data distribution, and are therefore better able to represent nonlinear and complex black-box models.

However, recent works have shown that local explainers can be inconsistent or unstable. For example, explainers may yield highly dissimilar explanations for similar samples [1,2], be sensitive to imperceptible perturbations [3,4,5], or lack stability under repeated application [6]. In high-stakes applications, it is imperative to give the user an understanding of whether an explanation is reliable, potentially problematic, or even misleading. One way to guide users regarding an explainer’s reliability is to provide corresponding uncertainty quantification estimates.

Explainers can be considered function approximators; as such, standard techniques for quantifying the uncertainty of estimators can be used to quantify the uncertainty of explainers. This is the strategy used by existing methods that estimate explainer uncertainty (e.g. [7,8]). However, we observe that for explainers this is not sufficient: in addition to uncertainty due to the function approximation of explainers, explainers must also deal with uncertainty due to the complexity of the decision boundary (DB) of the black-box model in the local region being explained.

Previous works investigating DB geometry have related higher DB complexity to increased model generalization error [9] and increased adversarial vulnerability [10,11]. Smoother DBs have been shown to improve feature attributions [12] and to produce more consistent counterfactual explanations [13]. [3] show that, in ReLU networks, samples with similar predictions can yield widely disparate explanations, which can be regulated through model smoothing. Consider the following example (Fig. 1): a prediction model is used for a medical diagnosis based on two features, cholesterol level and sodium intake. We use the gradient with respect to each feature as an estimate of feature importance. Patients A and B have similar cholesterol and sodium levels and receive the same prediction; however, the complex decision boundary (left) results in a different top feature for each patient. In contrast, the smoothed decision boundary (right) yields more consistent explanations.

We approach this problem from the perspective of similarity: given two samples and their respective explanations, how closely related should the explanations be? Following the intuition above, we define this similarity based on a geometric perspective of the DB complexity between the two points. Specifically, we propose the novel Weighted Exponential Geodesic (WEG) kernel, which encodes our expectation that two samples close in Euclidean space may not actually be similar if the DB within a local neighborhood of the samples is highly complex.

Using this similarity formulation, we propose the G aussian P rocess E xplanation Un C ertainty (GPEC) framework (Fig. 2), an instance-wise, model-agnostic, and explainer-agnostic method for quantifying explanation uncertainty. The proposed notion of uncertainty is complementary to existing quantification methods. Existing methods primarily estimate the uncertainty related to the choice of model parameters and fitting the explainer, which we call function approximation uncertainty, and do not capture uncertainty related to DB complexity. GPEC can combine the DB-based uncertainty with function approximation uncertainty derived from any local feature attribution method.

In summary, we make the following contributions:

- • We introduce a novel geometric perspective on capturing explanation uncertainty and define a geodesic-based similarity between explanations. We prove theoretically that the proposed similarity captures the complexity of the decision boundary of a given black-box classifier.

- • We propose a novel Gaussian Process-based framework that combines 1) uncertainty from decision boundary complexity and 2) explainer-specific function approximation uncertainty to generate uncertainty estimates for any given feature attribution method and black box model.

- • Empirical results show that GPEC uncertainty improves understanding of feature attribution methods.
